title: Going Up: Elevators
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history and mechanics of elevators, starting with ancient lifts and Archimedes, Louis XV's flying chair for Madame du Barry, and the 1850s rope-and-pulley passenger elevators. They cover Elijah Otis's 1854 safety brake demonstration (which they stress he invented as a safety device rather than the elevator itself), Otis Tufts's screw-driven elevator, how modern cable-and-counterweight elevators and governors/safety brakes work, the 1945 Empire State Building plane crash elevator fall, the small statistical risk of elevator death, elevator phobia and exposure therapy, personal space research, elevator etiquette (two-flight rule, holding doors, facing front), elevator traffic planning (probable stops, waiting time, handling capacity), and a listener email about an allergy episode that helped a child's sting reaction be caught early.

segments.title: Opening banter and Jerry's elevator rescue
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode and joke about Jerry being stuck for four hours in a crowded elevator with NASCAR fans and rescued through the top.

segments.title: Early lifts and Louis XV's flying chair
segments.summary: Ancient Roman lifts powered by people, livestock and water screws, with Archimedes mentioned. Louis XV's flying chair and flying tables are described, along with a tangent on the lazy Susan and dumb waiter.

segments.title: Hydraulic versus rope-and-pulley elevators and early dangers
segments.summary: Hydraulic piston elevators limited building height and were used in mansions. Rope-and-pulley passenger elevators took off in the nineteenth century but were dangerous because there was no safety mechanism when ropes broke.

segments.title: Elijah Otis and the safety brake
segments.summary: Elijah Otis and his sons created a spring-loaded safety device in 1852 and demonstrated it at the 1854 New York World's Fair. Hosts note he invented the safety mechanism that made rope elevators safe, not the elevator itself, and that the brake design is still used.

segments.title: Otis Tufts and the screw elevator
segments.summary: A different Otis, Otis Tufts, built an earlier elevator that ran on a threaded screw. It was safe but expensive and impractical, so it was not widely adopted.

segments.title: How modern elevators work and safety systems
segments.summary: Modern elevators use multiple cables looped over a sheave with a counterweight, driven by an electric motor. Governors trip wedges or brake shoes to grip the rails if the car speeds up, and buffers at the bottom absorb impact.

segments.title: Elevator falls and accident statistics
segments.summary: A free-fall scenario is discussed, including air cushioning and shock absorbers. The 1945 B-25 crash into the Empire State Building, where two cars fell from the 79th floor and one woman survived, is recounted. Hosts give a small per-ride fatality risk and compare escalator safety.

segments.title: Elevator door accidents and phobia
segments.summary: Hosts discuss rare door and movement accidents when getting on or off, and the advice to pay attention. They cover elevator phobia, its overlap with claustrophobia, and treatments such as exposure therapy.

segments.title: Personal space and elevator etiquette
segments.summary: Edward Hall's personal space categories and John Fruin's pedestrian planning handbook are discussed. Etiquette tips cover the two-flight rule, holding doors, stepping off in crowded cars, facing forward, and phone use.

segments.title: Elevator traffic planning and dispatch
segments.summary: Elevator designers calculate probable stops, waiting time, and handling capacity. Dispatch systems and sky lobbies are mentioned, and the hosts note differences between England, India, and China.

segments.title: Listener mail: allergy episode helped save a child
segments.summary: A listener writes that after hearing the allergy episode, her husband recognized a delayed allergic reaction in their son after a bee sting and got emergency care.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and invite contact through Twitter, Facebook, email, and the website.
